questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: That the university offered som courses that I found interesting (and enough different ones for me to have something to choose between) and that the location of the university was close to nature and outdoor experiences.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: UBC as a campus is well organized with many signs helping students find their way around, so I found it rather easy to navigate from the start. Moreover, I participated in an introductory activity organized by the university, which included a tour around campus and general information, which was both helpful and a good way to get introduced to other new students.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I found accommodation on campus through a Facebook group, which meant that my new roommates (who were on their 3rd year at the school) functioned as great helpers in navigating the new setting I had landed in. I could ask them any questions I had upon arrival and they'd explain and assist me in settling in. Other than that, Canadians are in general friendly and helpful, so whenever I'd be in doubt about something, I'd reach out to a stranger and ask them for guidance :)

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: It was possible to apply for on campus housing through the university's website, which around 50% of the applicants received. The rest had to find housing on their own either outside of campus or through students subletting on campus.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: I lived in an apartment with a kitchen, which is the case for most of the on campus housing opportunities for exchange students. Since I sublet a room in an apartment with students already living on campus, the kitchen was fully equipped. However, many of the exchange student residences have kitchens that are not equipped on arrival. Students moving into such places tend to go out with their new roommates (usually other exchange students) to purchase the basic necessities for their kitchen. As for meal plans I know that these are possible, but I do not know any exchange students using that option.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The solution I found is not that common (since most on campus exchange students get housing through the university and not through private posts), but I would have liked to know a bit more about the difference between living on campus versus off campus when having to apply for rooms, since deciding between those two options became difficult at a point. But at the end of the day, it is difficult to find housing in Vancouver and if you get any kind of offer or someone considering you for their room, you grab that chance - whether it be on or off of campus. In my case I really enjoyed living on campus, since it was extremely convenient to get to class and to participate in activities offered by the university. By not having to spend time in public transport getting to and from campus, I had a greater amount of time to do stuff outside of my classes. However, UBC is a big campus and has almost everything you need, which meant that many of the students living on campus rarely made their way outside of the campus area. Therefore I'd definitely say that there are perks of living off of campus as well, since you get out and explore the city more naturally and prevent living in the bubbly that campus can feel like.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I registered myself through the university portal, which works a lot like the one at UCPH. In my case I got all the courses that I wanted, but actually ended up changing a couple of my courses after attending the first classes of the semester either because I didn't like the course or found other courses more interesting.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I learned that even though a course is full, it is often possible to get a spot by writing and asking the professor directly. So even though you might not get granted a spot at first, try your luck by contacting the professor with a brief explanation on why you find their course interesting.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I managed to get a spot on all the courses I wanted, which I think is realistic when studying sociology, since many of the relevant courses accept a large amount of students.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Register for more courses than you might consider taking to ensure yourself a spot. You can always drop courses after a couple of lectures when you've gotten a better feeling of what you'd like to study. UBC has an add and drop period, which is exactly meant for changing around. However, some courses are really popular, so those might be smart to have signed up for before hand, since there might not be any spots left by the start of the semester.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I found the level different from the equivalent level in Denmark in two ways: Academically the level was generally a little lower than at UCPH, but since the requirements and expectations are very different, I'd say that studying at UBC was more demanding. Strangely enough I found 100 level courses more demanding not academically but practically than 200 and 300 level courses, since the teachers of the first year courses demanded a lot more participance in the classroom and weekly assignments were more common as well.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Some teachers require in class attendance and grade on behalf of your engagement in class. Moreover, quizzes and weekly tasks were a part of many of my courses, which meant that teachers expect you to have read your stuff and be able to participate in class discussions. I found that a lot more motivating than the teaching strategy at UCPH (at least for sociology students), since it makes everyone engaged in the classroom and gives you a better sense of whether you're understanding the material ongoingly instead of just testing your abilities at the end of the semester with no possibility of improving if you've misunderstood something.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I'd recommend taking the opportunity to try out courses outside of your main field, since it really (at least in my case) gives you some renewed energy school wise and a new perspective on a lot of the courses you've already taken in your own field.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The mandatory health insurance purchased through UBC at $325 and the U-Pass (for public transport in Vancouver) at $180.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I found myself going on many trips and some that were more expensive than I had planned for (surf trip, climbing trips, skiing trips), so these definitely made my exchange more expensive than expected (but were definitely worth it!). Furthermore, Vancouver is a really expensive city to be living in: Expect grocery shopping to be more expensive than is the case here at home (and more expensive than buying ready made foods), phone bills can easily cost you around 50 bucks a month and going out to bars you'll find your beers costing you quite a bit more than in Denmark as well. However, many facilities on campus are either free for students to use (aquatic centre, ice rink etc.) or fairly cheap to buy memberships for (gym, climbing wall etc.). So found myself being able to participate in activities around campus for a lot less of a cost than what I had expected :)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: UBC has a giant club universe, which I really enjoyed and took full advantage of! For every possible activity there is a corresponding club that anyone can join and in the first couple of weeks of every semester, the clubs arrange a big event with introductions to the different clubs and in many cases the possibility to do try outs in the different clubs around campus.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Personally I joined (and can highly recommend) the outdoor club (VOC), the salsa club and a couple of the activities arranged by the bike club (The Bike Kitchen). These clubs are a great way to meet new people and get activated from the moment you start at UBC. Moreover, many of the clubs worked as an introduction to Vancouver as a city and especially the outdoor club arranged many trips out of town as well and to fabulous spots around Vancouver, which was a perfect way to get a break from university life and get to explore some more of Canadas amazing scenery.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go on trips! Vancouver is an interesting city in many ways, but if you're into nature then take advantage of the many amazing places that are within reach just outside of the city. Whether it's just a day trip, a weekend or maybe a reading break, there are spots that are so worth visiting and so so close! Rent an evo with a bunch of fellow students or join the VOC (outdoor club) and tag along on trips already arranged by other adventurous students :)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I found that rather easy compared to other places in the world, where the culture is more different from the Danish.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Talk to your classmates :) From my experience many of the local students didn't necessarily have the time to engage in a lot of activities outside of school or in the clubs at uni, but the class room is a good mix of both local and international students, so that'd be the place to meet 'em :))

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The degree to which I would encounter homeless people in the streets of Vancouver. Canada has a huge problem when it comes to dealing with homelessness, food insecurity, and addiction, which was clear in particular parts of the city centre. Being a privileged young university student, I found that rather challenging to get "used to" or live with.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The friendliness of Canadians! Although most of the Canadians I met were on my trips outside of Vancouver, these people inspired me a lot by engaging in conversations so naturally and with such interest! So many times I found myself talking to complete strangers who'd tell me about their culture, their life or even their family history, which made me feel very welcome and safe throughout my exchange.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
First of all, be sure to save up a lot more money than you expect to use (Vancouver and British Columbia is expensive and wanting to see and experience everything while you're here doesn't make it any cheaper). 
Secondly, consider beginning you're search for housing well in advance - if you get housing through the university no worries, but in case you don't, start by becoming a member of the many different Facebook groups for housing in Vancouver and start looking at your options. 
Finally, know that you've chosen to study in a nature paradise, so if you're into any kind of outdoor activities, this is definitely the place to be! And be sure to bring any outdoor equipment you might have lying around at home, cus you'll definitely get a chance to use it while you're here :))

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Don't be too nervous about going so far away from home - UBC as a university takes good care of their exchange students and you'll get the chance to meet new people right from your first day of school :) And if you're looking for adventure, sign up for the outdoor club (VOC) cus they definitely are the easiest way to access amazing trip options and get to hang with lots of amazing people!
And be prepared, time flies by oh so quickly! Even though you may have so many plans and ambitions about what to experience and get done before leaving again, sit back and relax once in a while and enjoy wherever the weekends end up taking you and whatever the people you randomly meet and end up hanging out with have to offer :)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Volunteering at the Downtown Eastside Neighbourhood House on East Hastings once a week. If you want to get a closer feel of what the city is like from the perspective of less well of citizens and meet engaged and inspiring volunteers on a weekly basis, consider finding an organisation and joining them on some of their projects. This definitely gave me a completely different insight into what kind of city Vancouver was and what kind of initiative and lovely people that call it their home.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Slowing down. Dealing with fomo. To tell myself that I was doing all that I could to make my exchange as fun as possible and simultaneously letting myself slow down once in a while and enjoy doing nothing. So a piece of good advice: Whoever you end up spending your time with and whatever you guys end up doing, it won't compare with anyone else's experience of being on exchange cus it was your personal experience and what ended up being your adventurous four months away from home.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
